blocks.x: Today in the Seminar Room 2 of this library here, see Howard Tilton Library, Tulane University, and today is August the 14th, 1916, and what is your name please?
Pierre Merlin, Peter Merlin. I see.
How do you spell that last name?
M-E-R-L-I-N.
And your name?
Is Elizabeth Snaup.

And I'm Dick Allen. So we want to talk to you about, a little bit about your life, and then about the music you've played, and about the music in France in general that you've heard, not just that you've played. Where were you born?
In Bordeaux, in the southeast of France. And I went in Paris in 1942 for continuing my studies in art school, in fine arts school in Paris. I see.
What year were you born in, do you mind us asking?
When? Your birth date. Birth date, 1918. June 30. I see. And ask me.
What was the first music you remember as a little boy?

Oh, yes. I suppose I have a very confused remember of that. It was in 1925. I heard that I think it was an American jazz band in Vichy. In a resort, a town with water, special water for some cure. I was with my grandmother. And she brings with her in holiday. And in the casino in 1925. I'm not sure what year. It was maybe a year later or a year before, but about. I heard a jazz band with a Negro that plays saxophone and who walk between the tables. It's my first rim and branch of jazz music. I was seven years old about. And in my family, there were few records of not good jazz. It was a French reproduction of something about jazz. And then in 1935, about, I was in a fine art school in Bordeaux. And with friends that have records, they bring me with us, with them to hear the records. And I became very interested in jazz. And I bought records at that time. And then in about 1940 or 41, with the people, that men, we began to play between us. With who? With the people, with the friends, friends of a fine art school.
And did these people become professional musicians later?

One or two of them. Who were they? Or, now I don't know. One is a lawyer in Africa. One is a photographer. The other, I don't know. I don't know. And then I came in Paris, in Paris. And I was in art school for years. And I met Claude Luther, and I played with him and other friends for six years, from 1943 to 1949.

Under the Germans? They let you play jazz? The Germans? Germans? Allemands? No. I mean the Nazis did not stop you from playing jazz? They allowed jazz? I don't understand. Allemands? How do you say it? No, no. Deutsch? The Germans didn't stop you from playing jazz?

Oh, yes. Oh, it was the only place we can. It's in the basement of the jazz club in Paris. It was admitted, because there was no dance and no drink, and just cultural. And there were a few concerts in Paris with jazz musicians.
So the Germans, did the Germans like jazz?
A few, a few of them. But I met a German who was very interested. I can't remember his name, maybe it's Schulz.
Schulz Coren, Diedrich Schulz Coren.
Maybe. I can't remember. He was very interested in jazz. I know him. Oh, you know. Schulz, it's his name. Yes, he's a critic. He's on the radio now in Germany. Oh, yes. Oh, yes.
I never heard of him after that period. He's the one that the American troops captured him as an SS officer. Oh, yes.
I didn't know.
Yes, and the first thing he said was, where can I get some good Count Basie records? I didn't know. I didn't know. Yes. And so the Germans did not prohibit jazz in France?

They did not encourage him, but they had met in a few limits in concert or in the basement or the jazz club. They prohibit dance, of course. Why didn't they like dancing? What? They did not like? Oh, maybe them, but they don't want we dancing. Why? Why? They are victorious. It was an occupation. Yes.
So the French could not enjoy themselves?

Yes, but in a hidden place. There was parties at that time. There were parties. And it was not very usual, but I had, I was many times in parties to play or to hear music. I didn't dance, but I heard good records and something like that.
Did you have a teacher?

Not really. Not really. How did you learn jazz? A friend who had a teacher, he tried to teach me a little, but it was not very good. I had years of trouble with my lips and... I was not professional too. I made a sketch and painting at that time. It was just for the few years I played with God Luther, I made improvements because I play every day at that time.
Did you hear many American musicians before World War I? Before World War II?
No. In records, of course, but in person never.
What records did you listen to?
I was in Bordeaux before the war.
Oh yes. What records did you listen to?

Before the war, Armstrong O5, some Bigs by the Meck, and a few white bands. It depends. It was depending on the records that my friends had at that time. In Bordeaux, in a country, in France, before the war, it was difficult to have many records. There were a few records of good jazz in the shop. We had to write to have. It was not encouraging to us. About stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff stuff like stuff stuff stuff like stuff stuff stuff like stuff like stuff When did you move to Paris? 1942. I had a, I don't know the name, I won a sort of prize to go to Paris for three years.
Scholarship?
Scholarship. Scholarship.
For drawing, painting? Yes. Did you read music by the way at that time?
No, no.
Do you read now?
Even now. No. I try but I never succeeded. I never had enough courage to continue.
I see. Well, when you moved to Paris, could you hear more American records there?

Oh, yes. Yes, I went to the jazz club in Paris. They had many records. I said they had because every day a record disappeared. It was stolen. And in Paris, with Claude Luté and other friends of his band, we used to, once a week, to hear a very good record in a collector's house, Henri Bernard. And it was the very beginning of our knowledge of good jazz. And it was a nice man. And it was a very known collector in France. stuff like stuff few articles but it's a very nice money
well you uh
start
it out, did you play like anyone else? Did you imitate anyone in the beginning?
Oh, I'm not sure. I was, of course, influenced by the records I heard. Rex Stewart and Biggs Bayder Beck and Armstrong, of course.
And then after you moved to Paris, did you change your style at all?
I tried to be more close to King Oliver.
Did you play first trumpet or second trumpet with Luther? First, usually. First, usually. And that was King Oliver's part? Yes. I see. And what tunes did you play when you began with Luther? Yes.

I was very... cocktail at the beginning because we didn't know many tunes. But by the time we included more and more King Oliver tunes. And a few Jerry Lauren Morton tunes, Clarence Williams. And that's all. What's your favorite tune? Oh, King Oliver, of course.
He's your favorite trumpet player today?

I can say it's my favorite because there is Armstrong, too. But I think it's hard to tell which I prefer, because for me they are the giants of King Oliver, Armstrong, and Tommy Lanier, too. I like very much George Mitchell, too. I think there are the four men I prefer. I can give a place apart to Big Spader Beck.
What's your favorite title?
Title? Oh...
More so.
No, no, not one.
What are some of them?

Oh, no, I can't. I can't. You can't name several. All the King Oliver tunes I like, all of them. And many more tunes, too, and Clarence Williams. They are the base of my tunes, or repertoire in French. In English, too, we say that. Oh, yes. All right.
I see.
After the war, did many American musicians come to Paris?
Yes. The first I heard, I think it's a big band, who was not a new band. He had played many years.
A Negro or a white band? Yes.
Negro, yes.
Someone like Duke Ellington, or?
No.
Not that famous, or?

Don Redman. Don Redman. Don Redman. It's the first band I heard. And, of course, I heard Armstrong many times. And, the Xylophonist, as I am, Vibraphonist. Lionel Hampton. Lionel Hampton. I heard Lionel Hampton in a PX. It was a dance, a ball. I liked very much that evening. Mm-hmm. And... Go ahead. I tried to remember what orchestra I have heard. Oh, I remember in a very small auditorium, which was used during the war, when there was a piano, with Willie Smith, the pianist in Lionel Hampton. It was very pleasant. After the war? A very good concert. Yes. It was one of the first I heard. 1946, I think, or five, or five maybe.
So you appreciate other things than New Orleans jazz? Oh, yes. All the time. What do you like? What I like. Yes. Do you like blues? Big band swing?

Oh, I prefer the medium band, like King Oliver's band, you know, with two trumpets, clarinet, trombone, and four rhythm sections. I think it's, to me, the best balance combination, because it allows to have arrangements and some liberty to play. Not too rigid, not... I think it... For me, it's the best formula. Yes.
Well, what do you listen to? What? What do you listen to now, today?
Of course, I listen to everything, but I don't like everything.
What don't you like?
The same, I try to play.
Do you like Duke Ellington?
A little. I prefer Duke Ellington records of the twenties.
Do you like blues guitar and singing and all that? Yes, a little. I see. Bebop? No, not at all. Not at all. I see.
That bore me.
I wanted to ask you, who was in the Luther band when you started?
Who?
Who was in the Luther?

The name of the people, yes. And the instrument. Yes. Claude Luther, clarinet. Claude Rabani and me, the cornets. Mowgli, Jospin, and the trombone. He was, before he was in the trombone, he was a pianist, pianist in the band. I can't remember the name of the first trombone.
Did he record with you? No.

No, the other trombone. The first? The first trombone, no. Yes, yes, yes, but not public record. Yes, I see. And Christian Azzy, the piano, Claude Philippe Banjo, Michel Pacou, drum, and the bass, oh, the bass is Roland Bianchini. He's still playing with Luther. He's the only one that is still playing with Luther now.
Well, when you started, that's almost the same band that made recordings. Just one or two changes, huh?

We had about the same combination from 1946. The change was made after the summer of 1946. And from 1946, the end of the year, to 1949, it was almost that combination. Almost the same. Very few changes if one people was not available. But it was a rarity at that time.
Did any American musicians play with your band regularly?

Regularly, no. But in 1948, we were at the Festival of Jazz in Nice, in the French River. There was the Louis Armstrong Orchestra, and the Mesmes Roo Orchestra. And when we returned in Paris, the band of Mesmes Roo stood a little time in Paris. And for a week, each day of the week, we had the pleasure to play with Baby Dodds, Bob Roo, Bob Wilbur, Jimmy Archie. And I won once Mesmes Roo, but it was a week of enthusiasm to play with people like that musician.
What about Bechet?

I played a few times with Bechet, because it was in 1949. 1948 and 1949. I played in concert with Claude Lutheur, accompanying Bechet. But at that time, it was too much music to me to play every day. And we played at that time, the afternoon, the night, and sometimes the morning to rehearse and to recording. And I left the band because I prefer to draw and paint and make music for my pleasure. And the level of the orchestra went better, so I was afraid to be not able to follow.
I see.
I was afraid to play with Bechet. He was so great musician.
Did Nicholas play with you or any of those people?
Yes. Later, two or three times, with a different band, the band which I play now every Sunday.
And what band is that?

It's the band of Moglis Jospin, which was the trombone of Luther, with Rabanide, Claude Rabanide, and Pierre Atlan at the clarinet, and one man at the piano, Martin Morel. The rhythm section is very changing. I can't say a name because it's never the same. Yes, I see. But we'll try to do the same kind of music. And we had opportunities to play once with Bechet and twice or three times with Nicolas or other people. I remember we played two times with an American Negro singer, Billy Poole, who sings very well in the style of Bessie Smith. We played blues and old songs with him. It was very pleasant to us. How old? I think about 23. I'm not sure.
Do any of your musicians read in the band?
Yes, yes, two or three, more or less.
We call that spelling here.
Yes.
Not reading, but spelling.
Yes, because almost all the tunes we play, we never can find any sheet of music. So we learn about records.
Do you ever play for private parties?

Oh yes, sometimes for parties like in France, Saint-Catherine-et. It's an anniversary for the people and especially for the girls that are not married at 25 or after. It's a tradition. And it's a tradition in the girls that work in fashion, in suits for women. And usually at the anniversary they have a party and we played two times for these events.
